claims.text: A tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy made from low-activation elements can serve as a structural material for high-temperature plasma-facing components in fusion reactors.
The proposed alloy contains tungsten as a key constituent.
The proposed alloy has a multiphase microstructure.
The proposed multiphase microstructure is designed to optimize high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance.
A multi-principal-element microstructure provides a high melting point.
A multi-principal-element microstructure provides mechanical strength at elevated temperature.
A multi-principal-element microstructure provides irradiation resistance.
Using low-activation elements in the refractory HEA reduces the production of long-lived radioactive byproducts.
The combination of refractory elements in the HEA maintains structural integrity under extreme temperatures.
The alloy maintains structural integrity under neutron irradiation.
The high-entropy configuration produces microstructural stability.
Microstructural stability helps the alloy resist irradiation-induced degradation.
Microstructural stability helps the alloy resist void swelling.
The alloy will maintain mechanical integrity after prolonged high-temperature plasma exposure and neutron irradiation.
The alloy will retain low-activation characteristics after prolonged fusion-relevant exposure.
Refractory materials or HEAs not optimized for low activation may produce more radiological waste.
Existing refractory materials or HEAs may have insufficient high-temperature stability.
No direct experimental or computational evidence is provided for the proposed alloy's detailed composition or fusion-condition performance.
